newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Iraq sees early resumption of oil exports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Iraq sees early resumption of oil exports.

text.p: Iraq has stated its clear determination to resume exporting oil under a U.N. oil-for-food pact early next month, ending three weeks of uncertainty which had helped buoy sagging crude prices.

Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed, arriving in Vienna on Tuesday for the summer meeting of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), told reporters oil would start flowing once the fine-tuning of an aid distribution plan had been completed.
"We will start exporting oil when the distribution plan is finalised between the Iraqi government and the (U.N.) Secretary General...in 10 days we will start exporting oil, we hope," he said.

Under the terms of the accord implemented last December, Iraq is permitted $2.14 billion worth of oil over 180 days to raise money for food and medicine for its people suffering the effects of comprehensive sanctions imposed by the United Nations after Baghdad's invasion of Kuwait in 1990.

Iraqi exports during the first phase of the deal averaged 660,000 barrels per day (bpd) -- equivalent to the output of OPEC minnow Qatar -- but dried up in late May, just days before the renewal of the accord took effect on June 8.

Concern in Baghdad over the cumbersome aid plan and the slow pace of humanitarian deliveries -- more than half of the revenue raised in the first 180 days is still languishing in a Geneva bank account -- prompted Iraqi negotiators to delay delivering its distribution plan, one of the necessary steps before oil exports can resume.

Oil refineries, grown accustomed again to dealing with Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO), OPEC's second largest exporter before the Gulf War, felt the pinch as shipments from the Turkish port of Ceyhan and the Mina al-Bakr terminal in the Gulf stopped.

World oil prices rallied $1 a barrel between June 11 and June 17 and crude spot markets, particularly in southern Europe which took the bulk of the exports, strengthened dramatically as buyers scrambled for alternatives.

Benchmark North Sea Brent Blend crude for August delivery shed 11 cents to close at $17.88 a barrel on Tuesday in response to the news that Iraq could be exporting 730,000 to 750,000 bpd in a matter of days.
Traders in Vienna to negotiate contracts with SOMO said the modest price fall reflected continuing market concern that Rasheed's timetable may be over-optimistic.
Rasheed said no contracts for the second tranche of exports had yet been signed and that the price formulas were still being discussed.

Once Iraq's distribution plan is delivered to the U.N., the sanctions panel on Iraq, comprising the 15 members of the Security Council, must give its approval. The panel must also approve any new pricing formula and new contracts with oil companies.
The process can proceed quickly if panel members, particularly the United States, have no objections.
Rasheed said he foresaw no problems with any of these stages.
